strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated task: decoding text-specific information-seeking goals from eye movements in reading, with both selection and free-form reconstruction formulations.
Leverages the large-scale OneStop eye-tracking dataset with 180 participants, 486 questions, and critical span annotations, enabling extensive evaluation.
Provides a systematic experimental setup: 10-fold cross-validation, balanced splits, three generalization regimes (new text, new participant, both), and mixed-effects statistical testing.
Compares a broad set of models, including adapted state-of-the-art discriminative models and newly developed generative multimodal text+eye-movement LLMs, with informative baselines and ablations.
Reports above-chance performance on question selection, especially for RoBERTEye-Fixations, and shows meaningful progress on reconstruction in the new-participant regime.
Includes ethical considerations, reproducibility details, hyperparameter search spaces, and uses a publicly available dataset.
weaknesses: Overall decoding accuracy is modest for a top-tier AI venue: three-way selection peaks around 49% versus 33% chance, and the challenging same-span evaluation reaches about 57% versus 50% chance.

The newly proposed generative models are not the best performers on selection; DalEye-LLaVA is at chance, and DalEye-Llama underperforms the adapted discriminative model, limiting the modeling contribution.

In open-ended reconstruction, DalEye-Llama only marginally outperforms the text-only Llama baseline in the new-text regime on several metrics and trails the human same-critical-span baseline on BLEU, BERTScore, and QA accuracy.

The abstract's 'open-ended' framing is somewhat stronger than the evidence: selection is restricted to three candidate questions per paragraph, while free-form reconstruction remains difficult and is evaluated mainly with heuristic automatic metrics.
No human evaluation of generated questions is provided; reliance on BLEU, BERTScore, GPT-4o categorization, and a RoBERTa QA model may not fully capture reconstruction quality.

Some baselines are weak or at chance (e.g., reading-time embedding similarity), and the absence of a text-only selection baseline makes it harder to isolate the contribution of eye movements in the selection task.
Reproducibility is mostly described through hyperparameters and hardware, but no code repository is provided, which may hinder exact replication.

strengths: Introduces a challenging and potentially interesting task: decoding text-specific information-seeking goals from eye movements during reading, with both question selection and free-form question reconstruction formulations.
Uses a large-scale public eye-tracking dataset (OneStop) with critical-span annotations and a systematic 10-fold cross-validation setup covering new participants, new texts, and both.

Compares several discriminative and generative multimodal models and reports multiple evaluation metrics, including question-word agreement, semantic category, BLEU, BERTScore, and downstream QA accuracy.
Reports above-chance selection accuracy and some progress on reconstruction, especially in the new-participant regime, suggesting that eye movements contain useful information about reading goals.
Includes ethical considerations and a reproducibility statement, and relies on a publicly available dataset.
weaknesses: The core claim of open-ended goal reconstruction is weakly supported: in the new-text regime, generated questions often fall below human distractor baselines on BLEU, BERTScore, and QA accuracy, and can be no better than arbitrary or text-only baselines, so the central open-ended decoding claim is not convincingly demonstrated.

The task is not as open-ended or arbitrary as claimed: it uses a fixed set of three multiple-choice questions per text from OneStopQA, with two often sharing a critical span, and the reading context includes an upcoming comprehension test, which may introduce confounds.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior work on gaze-based task classification and reading-goal decoding; the paper mainly adapts existing models and extends earlier analyses rather than providing a fundamentally new methodological contribution.
Evaluation is limited to a single English eye-tracking dataset with native adult readers and Guardian articles, so generalization to other languages, populations, texts, and eye trackers is unknown.

There is no human evaluation of the generated questions, and the automatic generation metrics are weak proxies for open-ended reconstruction; QA accuracy can be high for generic or distractor questions, as suggested by the strong same-span human baseline.

Important controls and analyses are missing: no systematic text-only vs. eye-only vs. text+eye ablation for selection across all models, no feature-level ablation for eye-movement features, and no detailed error analysis across question types or readers.

Selection performance is modest overall: the best model reaches 49.3% versus 33% chance, and 57.3% versus 50% on the hard same-span split, which is not obviously enough to support the strong practical applications speculated about in the abstract and discussion.

The generative models are not competitive with the discriminative models on selection, and DalEye-LLaVA performs at chance, with little explanation for why one generative approach succeeds and the other fails.

The paper lacks a code release or artifact link, and model selection is performed on the full validation set across regimes, which may not reflect realistic deployment where the test regime is unknown.
Some statistical reporting is unclear or inconsistent, e.g., the chance/majority row in the main selection table includes significance markers, making the reported comparisons difficult to interpret.

strengths: Introduces a new and well-motivated task: decoding arbitrary, text-specific information-seeking goals from eye movements during reading, extending prior procedural goal decoding to semantic, question-specific goals.

Leverages the large-scale OneStop eye-tracking dataset and defines a thoughtful evaluation framework with question selection and free-form question reconstruction, including multiple generalization regimes (new text, new participant, both).

Adapts and compares several appropriate models, including strong discriminative baselines and two novel generative multimodal eye-tracking LLMs, with extensive hyperparameter and input-representation ablation studies.

Reports systematic results with confidence intervals and mixed-effects significance testing, and the best model (RoBERTEye-Fixations) achieves clearly above-chance accuracy, including on the difficult same-critical-span condition.
The paper is clearly written, reproducible in its setup, and includes an ethical considerations section that discusses risks, consent, and potential biases.
weaknesses: The dataset is limited to English Guardian articles and three candidate questions per paragraph; this constrains how truly 'open-ended' the goals are, since the selection task is a three-way choice and the reconstruction task is evaluated over OneStopQA questions rather than fully unrestricted reader goals.

The newly proposed generative models underperform the adapted discriminative RoBERTEye-Fixations model substantially on question selection, so the generative contributions currently serve more as proof-of-concept than as competitive decoding methods.

For question reconstruction, performance gains over strong baselines are uneven: under the new-text regime, DalEye-Llama is sometimes matched or exceeded by GPT-4o arbitrary questions or human same-span distractors on BLEU, BERTScore, and downstream QA accuracy, which weakens the claim of meaningful free-form reconstruction generalization.

Reconstruction evaluation relies on heuristic surface/semantic metrics, question-word/category agreement, and a RACE-trained QA proxy; these may not fully capture whether generated questions are valid paraphrases of the reader's actual goal, and no human evaluation of generated question quality is reported.

The paper does not evaluate real-time feasibility or practical applications, despite motivating assistive/educational use cases; this is acceptable for a proof-of-concept, but it leaves the practical implications aspirational.

strengths: Introduces a novel and cognitively meaningful task: decoding open-ended, text-specific information-seeking goals from eye movements in reading, going beyond prior work on procedural reading goals.

Formulates two complementary tasks (goal selection and goal reconstruction) and provides a systematic evaluation framework across multiple generalization regimes (New Participant, New Text, New Text & Participant).

Adapts and compares strong discriminative and generative multimodal models, including state-of-the-art eye-movement models and frontier LLMs, with appropriate baselines such as text-only models and human-composed incorrect questions.

Reports above-chance performance on the challenging goal selection task, especially when distinguishing questions with different critical spans, and demonstrates meaningful progress on the open-ended reconstruction task.
Ties model performance to cognitively interpretable gaze features (e.g., reading times before, within, and after critical spans), strengthening the scientific value of the work.
Provides detailed reproducibility information: public dataset, released code, hyperparameter search spaces, training details, and statistical testing.
Addresses ethical considerations including consent, privacy, potential biases for special populations, and the need for explicit user consent in future applications.
weaknesses: The abstract and introduction sometimes imply decoding 'solely from eye movements', but the models also receive the text and (for selection) candidate questions; the actual contribution is decoding goals from eye movements conditioned on text.

Goal reconstruction performance on new texts remains modest, with only small improvements over text-only baselines on several metrics, so the claim of 'considerable progress' toward free-form reconstruction may be somewhat overstated.

The feature ablation suggests that fine-grained fixation-level features add relatively little beyond the sequence of fixated words and linguistic features; a clearer pure text-only discriminative baseline would help isolate the unique contribution of eye movements.

The QA-accuracy evaluation for reconstruction depends on a RoBERTa model fine-tuned on RACE and excludes questions it answers incorrectly, which may introduce bias and limit interpretability of the measure.

The paper does not fully clarify whether the 'only linguistic text features' ablation includes the fixation sequence; if it does, it is not a true text-only baseline and the interpretation of feature contributions could be confounded.

strengths: Introduces a novel and scientifically interesting task: decoding text-specific information-seeking goals from eye movements in reading, moving beyond procedural reading-mode classification.
Leverages the large-scale OneStop Information Seeking dataset with hundreds of text-specific questions and critical-span annotations, enabling controlled evaluation.
Provides a comprehensive set of experiments across discriminative and generative models, multiple evaluation regimes (new participant/new text), and several generative metrics.

The best discriminative model (RoBERTEye-Fixations) performs above chance on all selection regimes, including the difficult same-critical-span condition, indicating that fine-grained gaze information may be useful.
Includes a cognitive interpretability analysis linking model confidence to reading-time effects before, inside, and after critical spans, which is a valuable direction.
Code and data are made available, and ethical limitations are discussed.
weaknesses: The central claim that eye movements alone enable decoding of information-seeking goals is not convincingly isolated. The feature ablation in Table 13 shows that a model with only linguistic/text features performs nearly as well as the full model (e.g., 48.6 vs 49.2 All), raising serious questions about the unique contribution of eye movements in the selection task.

No true text-only baseline is reported for goal selection. Without it, it is impossible to know how much of the above-chance performance is due to eye movements versus text/question-content heuristics.

Goal selection accuracy is modest: 49.3% in the 3-way task and 57.3% in the same-span task (chance 50%). The paper's claim of 'considerable success' overstates the strength of the evidence, especially for practical applications.

In goal reconstruction, eye-movement models often fail to outperform text-only baselines on new texts. For example, DalEye-Llama underperforms text-only Llama on question word and category accuracy in the New Text regime, and gains on BLEU/BERTScore/QA are small. This undermines the claim that eye movements provide robust open-ended goal information beyond text.

The few-shot Gemini prompt construction may leak information. For the New Participant regime, examples are drawn from the same paragraph but different participants; if any example contains the same target question, the model can copy it. This could inflate the reported New Participant few-shot numbers and is not adequately controlled.

The evaluation of goal reconstruction relies heavily on heuristic metrics (BLEU, BERTScore, question word, UIUC category). Human incorrect same-span questions achieve the best BLEU/BERTScore, showing these metrics reward lexical overlap and making semantic conclusions difficult.

The New Text & Participant regime contains only 10% of trials, leading to low statistical power; many reported comparisons are non-significant, yet the paper sometimes draws broad conclusions from them.
No human ceiling or human performance is reported for either task, so it is unclear how much room for improvement exists or what accuracy would be meaningful.

The open-ended aspect is limited: the selection task is 3-way multiple choice, and reconstruction results are weak in the most realistic new-text setting. The paper positions the work as a new challenge, but the demonstrated capability is currently narrow.

Model robustness is questionable: representation variations in the appendix (word-level vs fixation-level) cause dramatic performance drops, and the LLaVA variant mostly fails, suggesting the method is sensitive to modeling choices.

strengths: Introduces a novel and scientifically important task: decoding text-specific information-seeking goals from eye movements during reading, with goal selection and goal reconstruction formulations.
Uses a large-scale, well-annotated eye-tracking dataset (OneStop Information Seeking) with critical span annotations and careful evaluation splits across new participants, new texts, and both.

Develops and compares a strong set of discriminative and generative models, including adapted state-of-the-art eye-movement models and LLM-based approaches, with appropriate non-eye-movement baselines.
Goal selection results are convincing, especially RoBERTEye-Fixations achieving well above chance on same-critical-span questions, demonstrating fine-grained information in gaze behavior.
Provides cognitively interpretable analysis linking model performance to gaze features such as reading times before/within/after critical spans, strengthening scientific relevance.
Reproducibility and ethical considerations are thoroughly addressed, with public data, code, hyperparameters, statistical testing, and discussion of risks.
weaknesses: Goal reconstruction remains limited, especially for new texts, where improvements over text-only baselines are small or inconsistent; the claim of progress toward free-form open-ended reconstruction is somewhat overstated.

The Gemini few-shot New Participant setup may leak question identity: examples from the same paragraph but different participants could include the true question, potentially inflating few-shot results.

Reconstruction evaluation relies on heuristic metrics (question word/category, BLEU, BERTScore, QA accuracy) and lacks human evaluation of semantic correctness, fluency, or validity of generated questions.
Scope is limited to English, one dataset/domain, and predefined questions over paragraphs; true open-ended, arbitrary goals and broader generalization are not evaluated.

Some statistical analyses report extremely small p-values with very large N; effect sizes and practical significance could be clearer, and multiple comparisons across models/measures are not always corrected.

The paper uses 'open-ended' and 'arbitrary' goals, but the experimental setup still uses a fixed set of three candidate questions per paragraph and text-specific multiple-choice questions, so the open-endedness is constrained.
